activities.caption: true or false — the sketching craft
activities.name: protoSketchJudge

statements.s: Professionals sketch in thin, light construction lines first, then darken the confident lines.
statements.why: Proportions and major divisions first — the ink of the thought is not dry yet.

statements.s: One polished picture beats six rough variations early on.
statements.why: The rough variations force you to decide what actually matters — which is the point of sketching.

statements.s: Drawing two alternatives side by side turns a vague argument into a concrete comparison.
statements.why: And neither drawing looks finished, so the meeting stays about the ideas.

statements.s: Line weight works the other way round: heavy outlines for detail, light lines for the object's silhouette.
statements.why: Line weight shows importance — a heavy outline around the object, lighter lines for detail.

activities.anchor: edges that share a depth line up between plan and side
activities.caption: pair each drawing convention with its meaning
activities.name: protoConventionMatch

config.prompt: The language of making — pair each convention:

pairs.right: a centre-line — holes and axes of symmetry
dimensions placed clear of the geometry
the object looked at from above

config.why: Each view looks squarely down one axis, so every edge parallel to it appears at true length — no perspective, no foreshortening.

activities.anchor: a bad proportion was caught before any wood was cut
activities.caption: call the wedge's base depth
activities.name: protoWedgeEst

config.prompt: A phone stand leans at 15° from vertical with a 100 mm back edge. Trigonometry says the wedge base must run about how deep?
config.why: 100 ÷ tan(15°) ≈ 373 mm — obviously too deep; at 30° it computes to ≈ 173 mm, still deep, so the design became a two-part folding stand with a 90 mm base.
config.context: One sketch on graph paper, five minutes of arithmetic — the drawing doing its job.

activities.anchor: furniture instructions and engine manuals are exploded views doing their job
activities.caption: specify, explain or assemble? file each view
activities.name: protoViewSort

config.prompt: The pictorial family — file each fact:

items.label: true lengths a workshop can measure straight off the page
three axes set 120° apart, horizontals at 30°
circles become ellipses on tilted faces
parts separated along their assembly axes, each still aligned
stack-up order and which fastener goes where

config.why: Isometric drawings explain while orthographic drawings specify — and a good exploded view answers assembly questions before the workshop asks them.

activities.anchor: the design and the manufacturing instructions share one source of truth
activities.caption: fill the blanks — parametric CAD
activities.name: protoCadCloze

config.text: In %%0%% CAD you draw precise orthographic views with the software enforcing accuracy. In 3D parametric CAD the dimensions are stored as %%1%% values, not fixed ink — change the phone-stand width and the model %%2%%, the holes move with their faces, and the drawing views update themselves.
config.hint: Flat first, then the deep difference from paper — a model that rebuilds itself.

activities.anchor: the grip that stops fatiguing wins
activities.caption: walk the precious-model moment
activities.name: protoPreciousBranch

config.root: Mid-project, someone sands and paints the foam grip model so it looks great for the stakeholder demo. Walk it.

start.text: What just happened to the model?

choices.label: It became precious — the team will stop questioning it
choices.feedback: A model nobody questions teaches nothing — the risk arrived with the varnish.

choices.label: It got better — polish always helps
choices.feedback: Exploratory models deliberately avoid finish: it would make the model precious, and precious models end the questions.

before.text: The stakeholder demo is tomorrow. What do you bring?

choices.label: The rough set — plus a fresh stick taped with all three diameters
choices.feedback: Card, foam board, clay, wire and tape: fast to shape, fast to discard — the questions stay open.

choices.label: Only the polished one
choices.feedback: One defended model ends the exploration the whole kit existed to run.

done.text: Rough, disposable, held for a minute each: the demo becomes another round of the experiment instead of a verdict.

polish.text: Sanding and painting exploratory models is a waste — and worse, it makes them precious.

present.text: The demonstration now defends a conclusion the cheap material was never built to support.

config.why: Exploratory models investigate one aspect at a time in cheap material — the moment a model becomes precious, the team stops questioning it.

activities.anchor: a prototype is a nearly finished product, so teams postpone prototyping
activities.caption: the same flaw, two moments — drag the divider
activities.name: protoFlawCompare

config.prompt: When the flaw is found changes its price — drag between the moments:

before.label: Found in a paper prototype
before.text: Costs an afternoon — the design is still changeable, and the fix is a redrawn screen.

after.label: Found after tooling or launch
after.text: Costs a recall — the same flaw, priced at its most expensive moment.

config.why: Prototype early, prototype ugly, and let the polish arrive as the answers accumulate.

activities.anchor: to avoid conclusions the representation cannot support
activities.caption: sequence the decision loop
activities.name: protoLoopOrder

config.prompt: The loop that converges designs — put it in order:
items: Write the question — not 'test the design' but 'does the lid clear the hinge boss?'
Pick the cheapest representation that can answer that question
Declare what is fake — every prototype lies somewhere
Plan the discard — a prototype that cannot be thrown away will be defended
Run it again: question, build, test, discard or refine
config.why: The design converges through many small, cheap, honest failures — the way design-and-make projects always have.
